Surah al-Najm

Meccan. Its verses number sixty-two.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The first surah in which a prostration was revealed was ﴿By the star when it sets﴾. Mentioning him (ﷺ) by the title "your companion" serves to inform them that they are acquainted with the details of his noble conditions and aware of the excellent qualities of his exalted affairs; thus it is a rebuke to them in a more eloquent manner than naming him explicitly.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[3–4] ﴿Nor does he speak from desire.﴾ ﴿It is not but a revelation revealed.﴾ [al-Najm: 4]

The phrase "revealed" (yuha) is a descriptive clause emphasizing ﴿revelation﴾ [al-Najm: 4]. It removes the possibility of metaphor and conveys continuous renewal.

The pronoun refers to the Qur'an, as is understood from the context, and because the speech of the deniers concerned it. Some scholars referred it to whatever he speaks in general. They used this to argue that the sunnah in its verbal form is part of revelation (wahy, divine inspiration). They strengthened this with what is in the *Marasil* (mursal narrations) of Abu Dawud from Hassan ibn 'Atiyyah, who said: "Gabriel used to descend upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with the Sunnah, just as he descended upon him with the Qur'an, and he would teach him it as he taught him the Qur'an." The discussion of the Almighty's words:

[6–7] ﴿Endowed with power; then he stood firm﴾ ﴿while he was at the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 7]

﴿Endowed with power (dhu mirrah)﴾, with the mim pronounced with a kasra (mirrah), meaning firmness and solidity in his knowledge, such that it cannot change or be forgotten. The Arabs say of anyone of strong intellect and judgment: "dhu mirrah," from amrartu al-habl, when you twist the rope tightly.

﴿Then he stood firm﴾ ﴿while he was at the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 7]. Al-Zamakhshari said: he stood firm in his true form, not in the form in which he used to appear whenever he descended with revelation. He used to descend in the form of Dihyah. So the fa' (then) is, as its commentators have said, causal (sababiyyah), because his assuming of forms results from his strength and his capacity for extraordinary acts. Or it is conjunctive (atifah) with "taught him," meaning: he taught him in a form other than his original form, then he stood firm in his original form.

It has been said that "istawa" means "istawla" (took control), by his strength over the matters he was commanded to carry out. This was related by al-Qadi.

Al-Shihab said: al-ufuq is the direction (nahiyah), its plural being afaq. What is meant is the upper direction of the sky facing the observer, not the technical terminology of the astronomers. End.

Ibn Kathir said: His words, "Then he stood firm," refer to Jibril, peace be upon him. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. "While he was at the highest horizon" refers to Jibril standing at the highest horizon. This was said by Ikrimah and others.

Then Ibn Kathir said: Ibn Jarir has said something here that I have not seen from anyone else, nor has he related it from anyone. Its substance is that he holds that the meaning is: "Then he stood firm," i.e., this mighty, strong one, and your companion Muhammad (ﷺ), "at the highest horizon," i.e., they both stood together at the highest horizon, and that was the night of the Isra' (Night Journey). Thus he said, and no one agreed with him on this. Then he proceeded to justify what he said from the standpoint of grammar, and it is like His words: ﴿When we are dust and our fathers, shall we indeed be brought forth?﴾ [al-Naml: 67], where al-aba' (fathers) is conjoined to the pronoun in kunna without the explicit "nahnu." Likewise His words "then he stood firm." He said: al-Farra' related from some Arabs that they recited:

Have you not seen that the nab' tree stiffens its stalk,
while the brittle castor-plant does not stand firm?

What he said is grammatically sound, but the meaning does not support it, for this vision of Jibril did not occur on the night of the Isra', but before it, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on earth. Jibril descended to him, came close and drew near to him, in the form in which Allah created him, having six hundred wings. Then he saw him again on another occasion at Sidrat al-Muntaha, meaning on the night of the Isra'. This first vision occurred at the beginning of the prophethood, after Jibril, peace be upon him, had first come to him, and Allah revealed to him the beginning of the surah "Read" (al-Alaq). Then came the period of the interruption of revelation (fatrat al-wahy), during which the Prophet (ﷺ) went several times to throw himself from the mountain tops, and whenever he intended this, Jibril called out to him from the air: "O Muhammad! You are truly the Messenger of Allah, and I am Jibril." His heart would be calmed by this and his eye comforted. And whenever the matter lasted long for him, he would return to the same, until Jibril appeared to him while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at al-Abtah, in his form in which Allah created him, having six hundred wings, the immensity of his form filling the horizon. He drew near to him and revealed to him from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, what He commanded him. At that point he recognised the greatness of the angel who had brought him the message, the magnificence of his rank, and the exalted position he held with his Creator who had sent him. End.

I say: al-Qashani agreed with Ibn Jarir in the interpretation of the verse, and his words are:

"Then he stood firm": he stood firm in his essential form, and the Prophet was at the highest horizon, because at the time of the Prophet's being at the clear horizon, he does not descend in his own form, due to the impossibility of the pure spirit (al-ruh al-mujarrad) taking shape in the station of the heart, except in a form that suits the forms imagined in that station. For this reason he used to appear in the form of Dihyah al-Kalbi, who was among the most beautiful of people in appearance, and the most beloved of them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). For if he did not appear in a form that could be impressed upon the breast, the heart would not understand his speech, nor see his form. As for his true form in which he was created, it was not manifest to the Prophet (ﷺ) except twice: at his ascent to the Presence of Oneness (al-hadrah al-ahadiyyah) and the arrival of the spirit's station in its elevation, and at his descent from there and his return to the station at Sidrat al-Muntaha in the descent. End.

Likewise al-Mahayimi agreed with both of them, and his words are:

"Then he stood firm," and he, i.e., your companion, at the time of the standing firm of his self, became at the spiritual highest horizon. End.

Likewise Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, whose words are: It is well known that "huwa" refers to Jibril, and its implied meaning is: he stood firm as Allah created him at the eastern horizon, and he blocked the east by his magnitude. The apparent meaning, however, is that what is meant is Muhammad (ﷺ), and its meaning is: he stood firm in a place, and he is in the high place in rank and station, in elevation of status, not literally in occupying a place.

If it is said: How is this permissible when Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾ [al-Takwir: 23], indicating that he saw Jibril at the clear horizon? We say: In that passage too we say what we have said here, that he (ﷺ) saw Jibril at the clear horizon. A person says: "I saw the crescent," and it is said to him: "Where did you see it?" He says: "Above the roof," meaning the seer is above the roof, not the seen. And al-Mubin ("the clear") is the one that distinguishes, from abana (to make clear) a person, i.e., he is at the horizon that distinguishes between the degree of man and the station of the angel. For he (ﷺ) reached the limit and attained the furthest point and became a prophet, just as some prophets became prophets whom revelation came to in their sleep and in their form, while he was reaching the highest horizon and the horizon that distinguishes between the two stations. If it is said: What follows indicates contrary to what you hold, for His words: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ [al-Najm: 8] and beyond that, and His words, the Exalted: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13], ﴿at Sidrat al-Muntaha﴾ [al-Najm: 14], all of this indicates contrary to what I have mentioned? We say: We shall, if Allah the Exalted wills, show its agreement with what we have mentioned in its places, when mentioning its tafsir. End.

If it is said: The hadiths indicate contrary to what you have mentioned, since it is reported in the reports that Jibril, peace be upon him, showed the Prophet (ﷺ) himself in his form, and he blocked the east? We say: We did not say that it did not happen, and there is nothing in the hadith that Allah the Exalted intended by this verse that narrative, such that it would contradict the hadith. We only say that Jibril showed the Prophet (ﷺ) himself twice, spreading his wings, and he had covered and blocked the eastern side. But the verse was not revealed to explain that. End of al-Razi's words.

In al-Qurtubi there is a report of other sayings, and his words are:

"Then he stood firm," i.e., Jibril rose and ascended to a station in the sky, after he had taught Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Jubayr.

It has been said:

"Then he stood firm," i.e., he stood and appeared in his form in which he was created.

A third saying: the meaning of "Then he stood firm" is: the Qur'an became firm in his breast. On this view there are two possibilities:

The first: in the breast of Jibril when he descended with it, peace be upon him.

The second: in the breast of Muhammad (ﷺ) when it descended upon him.

A fourth saying: the meaning of "Then he stood firm" is: he became balanced, meaning Muhammad in his strength, and the second in his message. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

On the first view the complete sentence is "endowed with power," and on the second, "of intense strength."

A fifth saying: its meaning is "then he rose up." On this there are two possibilities:

The first: it is Jibril who rose up to his place, as we have mentioned just before.

The second: it is the Prophet (ﷺ) who rose up by the mi'raj (ascension).

A sixth saying:

"Then he stood firm," meaning Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, i.e., He settled upon the Throne, according to the saying of al-Husayn. End.

This is what we have come across so far of the sayings on the verse. The explanation of what we have chosen from among them will come at the beginning of the notes (al-tanbihat), and we have deferred mentioning it because of its connection to the verses that follow.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 53, verses 8–9:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[8–9] ﴿Then he drew near and came down, and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer.﴾ [al-Najm: 9]

﴿Then he drew near﴾ means: then, after his standing (in his true form), Jibril drew near to Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And came down﴾ means: towards him.

Ibn Jarir said: this is one of the postponed (al-mu'akhkhar) expressions whose meaning is preposed (al-taqdim). The original is in fact "then he came down and drew near," but the wording "drew near" was placed first because nearness implies descent and descent implies nearness, as one says: "So-and-so visited me, and he was good to me, and visited me."

Al-Shihab said: "came down" (tadalli) is a metaphor for clinging to the Prophet after drawing near to him, not in the sense of descending from a height, as is commonly held. Or it is a drawing near in the state of clinging, so there is no inversion and no need for the interpretation "he intended drawing near," as in (al-Idah).

﴿And was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer﴾ means: the distance between them was the measure of two bows, i.e., equal to them when stretched, or nearer. Or the pronoun refers to Jibril, meaning: he came close to him by about that much.

Al-Shihab said: qab al-qaws and qabbahu means the space between the bowstring and its grip (handle), and what is meant by it is a measure, for a bow is measured by it, as the cubit (dhira') is.

It has been said that it is inverted, i.e., qabay qaws (the two qabs of a bow), but there is no need for this. This refers to what the Arabs did in the pre-Islamic period: when they made a covenant, they brought out two bows and attached one of them to the other, so that the qab of one was adjacent to the other, until they were as if they were one qab. Then they would pull them both together and shoot with them a single arrow. This is a sign that the pleasure of one of them is the pleasure of the other and his anger is his anger, and opposing it is impossible. Thus said Mujahid, and the majority of exegetes approved it. End.

Al-Samin said: His words, exalted is He, ﴿or closer﴾ [al-Najm: 9] are like His words "or they increase" (aw yazidun), because the meaning is: he was, by one of these two measures in the view of the beholder, i.e., because of the closeness between them, the beholder is in doubt about it. This is a depiction of extreme nearness and of the certainty of his hearing what was revealed to him, that it was in the view of the eye and the view of the one standing by, as has passed in ﴿or they increase﴾ [al-Saffat: 147], for the meaning is: when the beholder sees them, he says: they are a hundred thousand or more.

It has also been said: "or" (aw) means "rather" (bal), i.e., rather closer.

"Closer" (adna) is the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil), and the thing compared to is omitted, i.e., or closer than the qab of two bows. His words, exalted is He:

[10] ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[12] ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾

"Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?" That is: will you argue with him and quarrel with him about what he witnessed directly, by seeing the angel who was sent down to him?

Al-Qashani said: That is, will you contend with him over something you neither comprehend nor are able to know or conceive? How then could you establish proof against him? What is required of others is to believe in it and submit to it, because the evidence for it has been established. In sum, the meaning is that disputation about what is seen is not valid, since argument is not permissible concerning things perceived by the senses, especially when the witnessing of them has been repeated, as he said:

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 53, verses 13–18 (part 1 of 2)**

**On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:**
[13–18] ﴿And He certainly saw him in another descent﴾ ﴿at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 14] ﴿near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [al-Najm: 15] ﴿when there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾ [al-Najm: 16] ﴿The eye did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17] ﴿Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18]

﴿And He certainly saw him in another descent﴾, i.e., another time of descending. The emphasis on this second vision is to negate doubt and suspicion about it as well, and to show that there was no confusion or ambiguity in it.

﴿at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 14], i.e., the place where things end. So al-Muntaha is either a noun of place or a mimi verbal noun (a noun formed with the prefix mim). It has been reported in the Sahih (authentic collection) that it is "a lote-tree in the seventh heaven, to which what ascends from the earth by the command of Allah ends, and from it is taken; and what descends from above it ends there, and from it is taken." 

Al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) said: "Perhaps it was called a sidrah (lote-tree) because it is a lote-tree, since people gather in its shade; that is, the lote-tree is a tree under whose shade people gather, and this one is where the angels gather, so it was likened to it and named sidrah for that reason. Its application to it is therefore by way of metaphor. However, it has been reported in a hadith that 'every lote-fruit on it is like a jar of Hajar,' so on this basis it is literal, and this is the more apparent view," as al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) stated.

﴿near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [al-Najm: 15], i.e., the garden to which the spirits of those brought near (to Allah) return.

﴿when there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾ [al-Najm: 16]. Al-Qashani said: "That is, of the majesty and greatness of Allah. Its meaning is that he saw Jibril (peace be upon him) at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, when the spirits and angels were covering it, descending upon it, and surrounding it from every side."

﴿The eye did not swerve﴾ [al-Najm: 17], i.e., the gaze of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not turn away from what he saw.

﴿nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17], i.e., it did not go beyond what was intended for him to see, but rather affirmed what he saw with certain, sound affirmation, free of any doubt. In this is a description of his good manners (ﷺ) and his steadfastness, for he did not exceed what he was commanded to see.

﴿Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18], meaning the angel whom he witnessed and who informed him of his prophethood. In this is the utmost magnification of his station, and that it was among the greatest signs.

Al-Nasir (Ibn al-Munir) said: "It is possible that al-Kubra (the greatest) is an attribute of ayat (signs), and the object of seeing is omitted to magnify and glorify the matter, as if He had said: 'He saw of the greatest signs of his Lord matters so great that description cannot encompass them.' Omission in such a context is more eloquent and more awe-inspiring."

**Points of note:**

**First:** We have mentioned, in the interpretation of His words, ﴿Then he stood﴾ [al-Najm: 6] ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 7], the many opinions of the exegetes (mufassirun), and it is not hidden that some of them involve artificiality and forced interpretation, such as the explanation of Ibn Jarir, al-Razi, those who agreed with them, and some opinions related by al-Qurtubi. The closest meaning of the verse is what Imam Ibn Kathir stated, as we quoted from him, because of the abundance of hadiths that explain it in this way. We say in support of this: the Qur'an explains part of itself by part, due to the similarity and resemblance of its noble verses. This verse is entirely similar to what is in Surah al-Takwir. For there Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ [al-Takwir: 19] ﴿of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 20] ﴿obeyed there and trustworthy﴾ [al-Takwir: 21] ﴿And your companion is not a madman﴾ [al-Takwir: 22] ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾ [al-Takwir: 23]. So you see these verses are similar to the verses here, although here there is an additional seeing and an explanation of nearness and approach that is not mentioned in (al-Takwir). The secret of the addition is the ascent of the Prophet (ﷺ) through the stages of perfection, time after time, and Surah al-Najm is among what was revealed after al-Takwir, as al-Suyuti related in (al-Itqan) from Ibn Abbas and other early scholars. Therefore, in (al-Najm) there is this additional honour and distinction. The essential meaning is this: what he speaks of from this Qur'an is not from his own desire, but is revelation taught to him by a noble angel, abundant in virtues, for he is of great power, possessing strength, of lofty standing at the highest horizon. Then, when Allah, Exalted is He, willed to send down His revelation to His Prophet, he descended from the horizon and drew near to him, being in the utmost nearness to him and able to see him and receive revelation from him. All of that is truth and sincerity, with no doubt in it. How can one dispute with someone who sees with his own eyes what his heart confirms and does not deny? Especially since his seeing was not a single occurrence; rather he saw him in a second descent, when he came down to him with the revelation in a specific place that is not confused for the one who sees it, namely the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. In sum, the agreement of these verses with the verses of (al-Takwir), by interpreting some of them by others, is a matter that is not obscure to the one who reflects. All of it is a refutation of the mushrikun (polytheists) who slander, and an affirmation of the reality of revelation and sending down, and the truthfulness of what he reports, especially since he is truthful in their eyes and they do not call him a liar. Nothing remains after obstinacy and denial except waiting for the sunnah (established pattern) of Allah regarding similar nations of disbelievers who rejected, as He indicated at the end of the surah.

This is a summary of the meaning of the verses. Anything beyond this is expansion, and carrying the wording to what its root permits. Whatever the wording can accommodate is what is intended, and Allah is the Granter of success.

**Second:** What we have put forward regarding the return of the pronouns in His words ﴿taught him one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5] etc., to Jibril (peace be upon him), is what the majority of exegetes relied upon, and we have supported it with what you have seen.

Imam Ibn Taymiyya said: "The nearness and descent in Surah al-Najm is the nearness and descent of Jibril, as A'ishah and Ibn Mas'ud said, and the context indicates it. For He said: ﴿taught him one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5], and that is Jibril; ﴿one of strength, so he stood﴾ [al-Najm: 6] ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ [al-Najm: 7] ﴿Then he approached and descended﴾ [al-Najm: 8]. So all the pronouns refer to this teacher, the mighty in power, who is one of strength, that is, of might, and he is the one who stood on the highest horizon, and he is the one who approached and descended. So there was from Muhammad (ﷺ) a distance of two bows' length or nearer. And he is the one who saw him in another descent, at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary; he saw him in his form twice, once on earth and once at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary." End of quotation.

Al-Bukhari related regarding these verses, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "He saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings."

At-Tirmidhi related from A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that he (ﷺ) "saw Jibril, and he did not see him in his form except twice: once at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and once at Jiyad (a place in Makkah), having six hundred wings, which filled the horizon."

As for what occurred in the hadith of Sharik in al-Bukhari, his saying: "The Mighty, the Lord of Honour, drew near and descended, until He was at a distance of two bows' length or nearer," if this is not an addition by Sharik, according to what Imam Muslim and others maintained, then it is a nearness and descent other than what is in Surah al-Najm. We believe in it and entrust its modality to Allah, Exalted is He, like all the attributes.

Ibn Kathir said: "Many people have spoken about the narration of Sharik. If it is authentic, it is to be understood as referring to another time and another event, not as an explanation of this verse, since the Prophet (ﷺ) was on earth and not on the night of the Isra'. For this reason He said after it: ﴿Then he approached and descended﴾, and this is the night of the Isra', while the first was on earth." End of quotation.

Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Bayhaqi said: "In the hadith of Sharik concerning the Isra' there is an addition beyond the position of those who claim that he (ﷺ) saw Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The statement of A'ishah, Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah, in interpreting these verses as referring to the seeing of Jibril, is more sound."

The scholar Ibn Kathir said: "What al-Bayhaqi, may Allah have mercy on him, said on this issue is the truth. For Abu Dharr said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Did you see your Lord?' He said: 'Light, how could I see Him?' In another narration: 'I saw Light,' related by Muslim."

As for His words ﴿Then he approached and descended﴾ [al-Najm: 8], it is only Jibril (peace be upon him), as is established in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from A'ishah and from Ibn Mas'ud. Likewise it is in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, and no opponent among the Companions is known for this interpretation." End of quotation.

Shams al-Din Ibn al-Qayyim said in (Zad al-Ma'ad): "The Companions differed as to whether the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord that night or not. It is authentically reported from Ibn Abbas that he saw his Lord, and it is authentically reported from him that he said: 'He saw Him with his heart (fu'ad).' And it is authentically reported from A'ishah and Ibn Mas'ud that they denied this, saying that His words ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ ﴿at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 13–14] refer only to Jibril. And it is authentically reported from Abu Dharr that he asked him: 'Did you see your Lord?' He said: 'Light, how could I see Him?' that is, the light came between me and seeing Him, as in another wording: 'I saw Light.'"

Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi reported a consensus of the Companions that he did not see Him.

Imam Ibn Taymiyya said: "Ibn Abbas's statement that he saw Him is not contradictory to this, nor is his statement that he saw Him with his heart. It is authentically reported from him that he said: 'I saw my Lord, Blessed and Exalted,' but this was not during the Isra'; rather it was in Madinah when he was delayed from them at the dawn prayer, and then he informed them of seeing his Lord, Blessed and Exalted, on that night in his dream. Upon this Imam Ahmad built, and said: 'Yes, he saw Him truly, for the visions of the prophets are true, without doubt.' As for Ibn Abbas's statement, 'He saw Him with his heart twice,' if his basis was His words ﴿And He certainly saw him in another descent﴾, followed by ﴿Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18], and the apparent view is that this is his basis, then it is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that this one seen was Jibril, whom he saw twice in the form in which he was created." End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir also said: "As for the hadith that Imam Ahmad related from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I saw my Lord, Mighty and Majestic.' Its chain of narration meets the conditions of authenticity, but it is an abridgement of the hadith of the dream, as Imam Ahmad also related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'My Lord came to me last night in the best of forms (I think he meant in sleep), and said: O Muhammad! Do you know what the Exalted Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la) are disputing about?' (The Prophet) said: 'I said: No.' So He placed His hand between my shoulders until I felt its coolness between my breasts, or he said my chest, and I knew what is in the heavens and what is in the earth. Then He said: 'O Muhammad! Do you know what the Exalted Assembly are disputing about?' I said: 'Yes! They are disputing about expiations and degrees.' He said: 'What are the expiations?' I said: 'Remaining in the mosques after the prayers, walking on foot to the congregations, and completing ablution in difficult conditions. Whoever does this lives in good and dies in good, and he will be as free of his sins as on the day his mother bore him.' And He said: 'Say, O Muhammad, when you pray: O Allah, I ask You for the doing of good deeds, the abandoning of wrongful deeds, the love of the needy, and when You intend a trial for Your servants, that You take me to You without being tried.'"

He said: "And the degrees are: giving food, spreading the greeting of peace, and praying at night while people are asleep."

Ibn Kathir then said: His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18], are like His words ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 23], that is, the signs indicating Our power and Our greatness. By these two verses, those among the People of the Sunnah who held that the seeing did not occur that night have argued, because He said: ﴿Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾, and had he seen Him, he would have reported it and said so to the people. End of quotation.

**Third:** Some scholars have held that this surah was revealed to establish the Prophetic Ascension (al-mi'raj al-nabawi), namely his (ﷺ) ascent, elevation and rising above the seven heavens, as mentioned in the hadiths of the mi'raj: at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary above the heavens, and the witnessing of Jibril in his form.

Al-Qalyubi said: Since the Night Journey (al-isra') preceded the Ascension (al-mi'raj) in existence, as it serves as a means and a proof, for believing in the supernatural events within it necessarily entails believing in the Ascension and what it contains. And since the supernatural events in the Ascension were greater and more numerous, God, exalted is He, began with an oath that indicates the confirmation of its establishment and a rebuttal of those who deny it and attack it. Along with that rebuttal, He digressed to refute those who attributed to him (ﷺ) what is not permissible for him, saying: ﴿By the star﴾ [al-Najm: 1], etc. End of quotation.

(p-5569) From what we have presented, it becomes clear that the revelation of the surah was to confirm the Prophetic message and to verify the revelation, that it is the teaching of a noble angel, seen by the Prophetic presence with a vision that dispels every doubt, not to establish the Ascension.

Furthermore, among the strange things here is the statement of some people, trying to discover the secret of separating the Night Journey from the Ascension and mentioning each in a separate surah, which in its example is: The Night Journey was revealed first on its own, to lead the polytheists to accept what the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) in it had made clear, as a means toward believing in what lies beyond it. For he (ﷺ) was directed to inform the polytheists first about the Night Journey to the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa), because the Quraysh knew it, so they would ask him about it, and he would inform them of what they knew, while they knew that he (ﷺ) had never entered Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) at all, and thus the proof would be established against them.

And so it happened, as mentioned in the narrations. Following this announcement, the explanation of the Night Journey was revealed. Then he (ﷺ) was inspired to inform them of the Ascension to the dominion of the heavens (malakut al-samawat) and the seeing of Jibril (peace be upon him), and God revealed his confirmation in the surah of al-Najm. End of quotation. All of this has no chain of transmission (sanad) to support it. Yes! Al-Bayhaqi, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir narrated in a lengthy hadith that he (ﷺ) arose in Makkah informing them of wonders: "Indeed I came last night to Bayt al-Maqdis, and I was taken up to the heaven, and I saw such and such," except that it may be said: this is not among the narrations of the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and there is no proof in reports except those narrated by the two of them.

In sum, what is relied upon is that the Ascension is not mentioned in the Qur'an at all, and what is mentioned in this surah and in the surah of al-Takwir has no connection to the Ascension; rather, it is the Prophet's vision of Jibril from the earth in his true form, as has preceded. As for the Ascension, it was a spiritual dream vision (ru'ya manamiyya ruhaniyya), as is clear from the hadith of al-Bukhari on this matter through its chains that go back to Anas and Malik ibn Abi Sa'sa'a. Some have said: That is why it is not mentioned in the hadith of the Ascension, according to the narration of al-Bukhari, which is among the most authentic narrations by scholarly consensus (ijma'), that the Prophet (ﷺ) traveled first to Bayt al-Maqdis; rather, what is mentioned in it is that he traveled directly from Makkah to the first heaven. Likewise, it does not mention that Jibril left him and then appeared to him at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha) in his true form; rather, what is mentioned is that he accompanied him from the beginning of the Ascension to its end in one single form. This indicates that what the Qur'an mentions as having occurred while awake is other than what is mentioned in the hadith as having occurred in a dream at another time, (p-5570) otherwise both would have been mentioned together in a single context, either in the Qur'an or in the most authentic hadiths. And this matter has not occurred except in some narrations that are not relied upon, which result from some narrators mixing up events, some with others. End of quotation, and God knows best.

And since the supernatural events in the Ascension were greater and more numerous, God, exalted is He, began with an oath that indicates the confirmation of its establishment and a rebuttal of those who deny it and attack it. Along with that rebuttal, He digressed to refute those who attributed to him (ﷺ) what is not permissible for him, saying: ﴿By the star﴾ [al-Najm: 1], etc. End of quotation.

(p-5569) From what we have presented, it becomes clear that the revelation of the surah was to confirm the Prophetic message and to verify the revelation, that it is the teaching of a noble angel, seen by the Prophetic presence with a vision that dispels every doubt, not to establish the Ascension.

Furthermore, among the strange things here is the statement of some people, trying to discover the secret of separating the Night Journey from the Ascension and mentioning each in a separate surah, which in its example is: The Night Journey was revealed first on its own, to lead the polytheists to accept what the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) in it had made clear, as a means toward believing in what lies beyond it. For he (ﷺ) was directed to inform the polytheists first about the Night Journey to the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa), because the Quraysh knew it, so they would ask him about it, and he would inform them of what they knew, while they knew that he (ﷺ) had never entered Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) at all, and thus the proof would be established against them.

And so it happened, as mentioned in the narrations. Following this announcement, the explanation of the Night Journey was revealed. Then he (ﷺ) was inspired to inform them of the Ascension to the dominion of the heavens (malakut al-samawat) and the seeing of Jibril (peace be upon him), and God revealed his confirmation in the surah of al-Najm. In sum, what is relied upon is that the Ascension is not mentioned in the Qur'an at all, and what is mentioned in this surah and in the surah of al-Takwir has no connection to the Ascension; rather, it is the Prophet's vision of Jibril from the earth in his true form, as has preceded. As for Ibn Abbas's statement, 'He saw Him with his heart twice,' if his basis was His words ﴿And He certainly saw him in another descent﴾, followed by ﴿Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18], and the apparent view is that this is his basis, then it is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that this one seen was Jibril, whom he saw twice in the form in which he was created." Al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) said: "Perhaps it was called a sidrah (lote-tree) because it is a lote-tree, since people gather in its shade; that is, the lote-tree is a tree under whose shade people gather, and this one is where the angels gather, so it was likened to it and named sidrah for that reason. Its application to it is therefore by way of metaphor. However, it has been reported in a hadith that 'every lote-fruit on it is like a jar of Hajar,' so on this basis it is literal, and this is the more apparent view," as al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) stated.

﴿near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [al-Najm: 15], i.e., the garden to which the spirits of those brought near (to Allah) return.

﴿when there covered the Lote-tree that which covered﴾ [al-Najm: 16]. Al-Qashani said: "That is, of the majesty and greatness of Allah. The secret of the addition is the ascent of the Prophet (ﷺ) through the stages of perfection, time after time, and Surah al-Najm is among what was revealed after al-Takwir, as al-Suyuti related in (al-Itqan) from Ibn Abbas and other early scholars. Therefore, in (al-Najm) there is this additional honour and distinction. The essential meaning is this: what he speaks of from this Qur'an is not from his own desire, but is revelation taught to him by a noble angel, abundant in virtues, for he is of great power, possessing strength, of lofty standing at the highest horizon. Then, when Allah, Exalted is He, willed to send down His revelation to His Prophet, he descended from the horizon and drew near to him, being in the utmost nearness to him and able to see him and receive revelation from him. All of that is truth and sincerity, with no doubt in it. How can one dispute with someone who sees with his own eyes what his heart confirms and does not deny? Especially since his seeing was not a single occurrence; rather he saw him in a second descent, when he came down to him with the revelation in a specific place that is not confused for the one who sees it, namely the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. In sum, the agreement of these verses with the verses of (al-Takwir), by interpreting some of them by others, is a matter that is not obscure to the one who reflects. All of it is a refutation of the mushrikun (polytheists) who slander, and an affirmation of the reality of revelation and sending down, and the truthfulness of what he reports, especially since he is truthful in their eyes and they do not call him a liar. Nothing remains after obstinacy and denial except waiting for the sunnah (established pattern) of Allah regarding similar nations of disbelievers who rejected, as He indicated at the end of the surah.

This is a summary of the meaning of the verses. Anything beyond this is expansion, and carrying the wording to what its root permits. Whatever the wording can accommodate is what is intended, and Allah is the Granter of success.

And since the supernatural events in the Ascension were greater and more numerous, God, exalted is He, began with an oath that indicates the confirmation of its establishment and a rebuttal of those who deny it and attack it. Along with that rebuttal, He digressed to refute those who attributed to him (ﷺ) what is not permissible for him, saying: ﴿By the star﴾ [al-Najm: 1], etc. End of quotation.

(p-5569) From what we have presented, it becomes clear that the revelation of the surah was to confirm the Prophetic message and to verify the revelation, that it is the teaching of a noble angel, seen by the Prophetic presence with a vision that dispels every doubt, not to establish the Ascension.

Furthermore, among the strange things here is the statement of some people, trying to discover the secret of separating the Night Journey from the Ascension and mentioning each in a separate surah, which in its example is: The Night Journey was revealed first on its own, to lead the polytheists to accept what the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) in it had made clear, as a means toward believing in what lies beyond it. For he (ﷺ) was directed to inform the polytheists first about the Night Journey to the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa), because the Quraysh knew it, so they would ask him about it, and he would inform them of what they knew, while they knew that he (ﷺ) had never entered Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) at all, and thus the proof would be established against them.

And so it happened, as mentioned in the narrations. Following this announcement, the explanation of the Night Journey was revealed. He said: "And the degrees are: giving food, spreading the greeting of peace, and praying at night while people are asleep."

Ibn Kathir then said: His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18], are like His words ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 23], that is, the signs indicating Our power and Our greatness. Then God, exalted is He, said, denouncing the polytheists for their worship of idols and their taking houses for them, in imitation of the Ka'bah which was built by the Friend of the Most Merciful (Khalil al-Rahman) for the worship of Him alone, with His saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 53, verses 19–20:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[19–20] ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza? And Manat, the third, the other one?﴾ [An-Najm: 20]

﴿Have you considered al-Lat?﴾ Ibn Kathir said: It is a white rock, carved, and upon it is a house at al-Ta'if which has curtains and custodians (sadana), and around it is a courtyard held in reverence by the people of al-Ta'if, who are Thaqif and those who follow them. They took pride in it over the other tribes of the Arabs after Quraysh. Ibn Jarir said: They had derived its name from the name of Allah, so they said "al-Lat," meaning its feminine form from His name, exalted is Allah far above what they say, highly exalted. This is like their saying "Amr" and "Amra."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is of the pattern fa'lah from (lawa), because they used to turn (yalwuna) around it and devote themselves to worship there (ya'kufuna li-l-'ibadah), or they used to wind (yaltawuna) around it, i.e., they circumambulated it.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Rabi' ibn Anas that they read (al-Lātt) with a doubled taa', and they explained it as meaning that he was a man who used to knead (yaluttu) sawiq (a porridge of parched grain) for the pilgrims in the Jahiliyyah; when he died, they devoted themselves to his grave and worshipped him.

As for al-'Uzza, it is a tree upon which there is a building and curtains at Nakhla, which lies between Makkah and al-Ta'if.

Ibn Jarir said: They derived its name from His name al-'Aziz (the Mighty), and al-Zamakhshari said: Its origin is the feminine of al-A'azz (the mightiest).

(p-5571) ﴿And Manat, the third, the other one﴾ [An-Najm: 20]. It is a rock that was at al-Mushallal near Qudayd, between Makkah and Madinah, and Khuza'ah, al-Aws and al-Khazraj in their Jahiliyyah used to venerate it and would assume the state of ihram from it for the Hajj to the Ka'bah.

Al-Bukhari related a similar report from 'A'ishah.

Ibn Jarir said: Some of the people knowledgeable in the language of the Arabs from among the people of Basra used to say: "al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat, the third," are idols of stone that were inside the Ka'bah, which they worshipped. End of quote.

Remarks:

The first: The judge (al-Qadi) said: (Manat) is of the pattern fa'alah from manah, meaning he cut it off, for they used to slaughter sacrificial animals at it. From this the name (Mina) is derived, because sacrificial animals are cut there (yumannaa), i.e., slaughtered.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It seems it was named Manat because the blood of the rites used to be poured out (tumanna) at it, i.e., shed. It is also read Munā'ah, of the pattern mufa'alah, from (al-nawʾ), as if they used to seek rain by the rising stars there, seeking blessing through it.

If it is said: That its being "third" and "other" is distinct from what preceded it is known and does not need clarification.

It is answered: These are two epithets for emphasis, or "third" is for emphasis and "other" explains it, because it is ranked lower in their estimation than al-Lat and al-Uzza.

Al-Nasir said: "Al-ukhra" is what comes last, and there is no doubt that it is originally derived from existential posteriority (al-ta'khir al-wujudi), but the Arabs turned it away from use in existential posteriority to use where a previously mentioned item is merely contrasted, until it lost its indication of the original meaning. This is unlike "akhar" and "akhirah" on the pattern fa'il and fa'ilah, for their indication of existential posteriority remains unchanged. Hence they avoided saying "Rabi' al-Akhar" on the pattern af'al, and "Jumada al-Ukhra," and instead said "Rabi' al-Akhir" on the pattern fa'il, and "Jumada al-Akhirah" on the pattern fa'ilah, because they wanted to convey existential posteriority, since the afal and fu'la forms from this derivation have lost their indication of their purpose; so they turned away from them to al-akhar (p-5572) and al-akhirah and adhered to that in both. This is a question which Shaykh Abu 'Amr ibn al-Hajib, may Allah have mercy on him, had clarified at the end of his life, and it is the truth, Allah willing. In that case, the intended meaning is an indication of a distinct prior mention, together with what we believe concerning the completion of the verse's end-rhyme. End of quote.

The second: Ibn Kathir said: In the Arabian Peninsula and elsewhere there were other taghut (idols) that the Arabs venerated in the same way as the Ka'bah, apart from these three which are specified in His Mighty Book, and He singled out these for mention only because they are more famous than others.

Ibn Ishaq said in (al-Sirah): The Arabs had taken, alongside the Ka'bah, taghut, which are houses they venerated as they venerated the Ka'bah; they had custodians and curtains, gifts were offered to them as gifts were offered to the Ka'bah, they circumambulated them as they circumambulated it, and they slaughtered at them, though they knew the Ka'bah's virtue over them, that it was known to be the House of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his mosque. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to it, and he destroyed it, saying:

O Uzza, disbelief in you! No glorification of you! Indeed I see that Allah has humiliated you.

Al-Nasa'i related from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to Nakhla, where al-Uzza was. Then he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: 'Return, for you have done nothing.' Khalid returned, and when he saw the custodians, who were its guardians, they exerted themselves in tricks, saying: 'O Uzza! O Uzza!' Khalid came to it, and there was a naked woman with disheveled hair putting dust on her head, so he struck her with the sword until he killed her. Then he returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: 'That was al-Uzza.'"

Ibn Ishaq said: Al-Lat belonged to Thaqif at al-Ta'if, and its custodians and guardians were Banu Mu'tab. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah and Abu Sufyan Sakhr ibn Harb to it, and they demolished it and made in its place a mosque at al-Ta'if.

(p-5573) Ibn Ishaq said: Manat belonged to al-Aws and al-Khazraj and those who followed their religion from the people of Yathrib, on the seacoast, on the side of al-Mushallal near Qudayd. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abu Sufyan Sakhr ibn Harb to it, and he demolished it. It is said: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. End of quote.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[21–22] ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female? That, then, is an unjust division.﴾ [al-Najm: 22]

﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: They used to say that the angels and these idols are the daughters of God, and they worshipped them, claiming that they were their intercessors with God, Exalted is He, while they buried their daughters alive. So it was said to them: ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ It is also possible that what is meant is that al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are females, (p-5574) and you have made them partners with God, and it is among your traits to despise females and to disdain that they be born to you and be attributed to you. So how do you make these females equals to God and call them gods? End of quotation.

A subtle point:

Al-Shihab said: The discussion of (ara'ayta) has passed many times, and that it means (akhbarani, "tell me"), and on how it indicates that, and the disagreement of the grammarians concerning the verb of seeing in it, whether it is visual. In that case the interrogative clause after it is resumed to explain the one being asked about. This is what al-Radi chose. Or it is cognitive, in which case it occupies the position of the second object, and the linking element then is that it is in the sense of: "Are they the daughters of God?"

Al-Samin said: It seems the original structure was: "Is for you the male, and for Him they (i.e., those idols)?" This noun was preferred to the pronoun because it falls at the end of a verse-ending (fasila).

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿That﴾ [al-Najm: 22] refers to the division understood from the interrogative clause. ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾ [al-Najm: 22], i.e., oppressive, not equitable, deficient and not complete, because you have assigned to your Lord offspring and equals that you dislike for yourselves, and you have preferred yourselves with what you are pleased with.

Ibn Jarir said: The Arabs say (dazatuhu haqqahu) with a kasra on the dad, and (duzatuhu) with a damma, so I "adhiduhu" and "adhuzuhu," and that is when you diminish his right and withhold it.

Note:

Al-Samin said: Ibn Kathir recited ﴿di'za﴾ with a silent hamza, and the rest recited with a ya' in its place. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited ﴿daya﴾ with a fatha on the dad and the ya' silent. As for the recitation of the majority, it may be from (daza'hu yadiduhu), when he oppressed him and was unjust toward him, so the meaning of (diza) is "unjust." On this basis it has two possible readings:

One of them: that it is an adjective on the pattern (fu'la) with a damma on the fa', but the fa' was given a kasra so that the ya' would be sound, as in (bayd).

If it is asked: What necessity is there to assume its original form had a damma on the fa', and why was it not said (fi'la) with a kasra?

The answer: Sibawayh related that the pattern (fi'la) with a kasra on the fa' did not occur among adjectives; rather it occurred with a damma, such as (hubla), (unthá), (ruba) and the like. However, others related that form in adjectives: Tha'lab related: "mishyatun hiykan" and "rajulun kaysan." Others related: "imra'atun 'izhan" and "imra'atun si'lan." This does not refute Sibawayh, because he would say of (hiykan and kaysan) what he says of (diza), to make the ya' sound. As for 'izhan and si'lan, the well-known forms are 'izhat and si'lat.

The second possibility: that it is a verbal noun like (dhikra). Al-Kisa'i said: It is said (daza yadizu dizan), like (dhakara yadhkuru dhikran). It may also be from (da'aza) with a hamza, as in Ibn Kathir's reading, except that he lightened its hamza into a ya'. Although it is not among the practices of all the reciters to change such a hamza into a ya', this is a dialect that was adopted, so they recited with it. The meaning of (da'aza yad'azu) with a hamza is to diminish something by wrong and oppression, and this is close to the first meaning. And (diza) in Ibn Kathir's reading is a verbal noun described by the adjective, and it is not an original adjective, because of what has preceded from Sibawayh.

If it is asked: Why was it not said of (di'za) with a kasra and a hamza that its origin is (diza) with a damma, so the fa' was given a kasra as was said with the ya'? The answer: There is no reason here for change, since the damma with a hamza is not as burdensome as with a silent ya'. And it was heard from them: (du'uza) with a damma on the dad together with a waw and a hamza.

As for Zayd's reading, it may be a verbal noun described by the adjective, like (da'wa), or an adjective like (kisra) and (atsha). End of quotation.

Al-Shihab said: The discussion of (ara'ayta) has passed many times, and that it means (akhbarani, "tell me"), and on how it indicates that, and the disagreement of the grammarians concerning the verb of seeing in it, whether it is visual. In that case the interrogative clause after it is resumed to explain the one being asked about. This is what al-Radi chose. Or it is cognitive, in which case it occupies the position of the second object, and the linking element then is that it is in the sense of: "Are they the daughters of God?"

Al-Samin said: It seems the original structure was: "Is for you the male, and for Him they (i.e., those idols)?" This noun was preferred to the pronoun because it falls at the end of a verse-ending (fasila).

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿That﴾ [al-Najm: 22] refers to the division understood from the interrogative clause. ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾ [al-Najm: 22], i.e., oppressive, not equitable, deficient and not complete, because you have assigned to your Lord offspring and equals that you dislike for yourselves, and you have preferred yourselves with what you are pleased with.

Ibn Jarir said: The Arabs say (dazatuhu haqqahu) with a kasra on the dad, and (duzatuhu) with a damma, so I "adhiduhu" and "adhuzuhu," and that is when you diminish his right and withhold it.

Note:

Al-Samin said: Ibn Kathir recited ﴿di'za﴾ with a silent hamza, and the rest recited with a ya' in its place. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited ﴿daya﴾ with a fatha on the dad and the ya' silent. As for the recitation of the majority, it may be from (daza'hu yadiduhu), when he oppressed him and was unjust toward him, so the meaning of (diza) is "unjust." On this basis it has two possible readings:

One of them: that it is an adjective on the pattern (fu'la) with a damma on the fa', but the fa' was given a kasra so that the ya' would be sound, as in (bayd).

If it is asked: What necessity is there to assume its original form had a damma on the fa', and why was it not said (fi'la) with a kasra?

The answer: Sibawayh related that the pattern (fi'la) with a kasra on the fa' did not occur among adjectives; rather it occurred with a damma, such as (hubla), (unthá), (ruba) and the like. However, others related that form in adjectives: Tha'lab related: "mishyatun hiykan" and "rajulun kaysan." Others related: "imra'atun 'izhan" and "imra'atun si'lan." This does not refute Sibawayh, because he would say of (hiykan and kaysan) what he says of (diza), to make the ya' sound. As for 'izhan and si'lan, the well-known forms are 'izhat and si'lat.

The second possibility: that it is a verbal noun like (dhikra). Al-Kisa'i said: It is said (daza yadizu dizan), like (dhakara yadhkuru dhikran). It may also be from (da'aza) with a hamza, as in Ibn Kathir's reading, except that he lightened its hamza into a ya'. Although it is not among the practices of all the reciters to change such a hamza into a ya', this is a dialect that was adopted, so they recited with it. The meaning of (da'aza yad'azu) with a hamza is to diminish something by wrong and oppression, and this is close to the first meaning. And (diza) in Ibn Kathir's reading is a verbal noun described by the adjective, and it is not an original adjective, because of what has preceded from Sibawayh.

If it is asked: Why was it not said of (di'za) with a kasra and a hamza that its origin is (diza) with a damma, so the fa' was given a kasra as was said with the ya'? The answer: There is no reason here for change, since the damma with a hamza is not as burdensome as with a silent ya'. And it was heard from them: (du'uza) with a damma on the dad together with a waw and a hamza.

As for Zayd's reading, it may be a verbal noun described by the adjective, like (da'wa), or an adjective like (kisra) and (atsha). End of quotation.

The commentary on the Almighty's saying:

[23] ﴿They are but names that you and your fathers have named; God has sent down no authority for them. They follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire, though guidance has already come to them from their Lord.﴾

﴿They are﴾, that is, the idols mentioned, with regard to the divinity they claim for them. ﴿but names﴾, that is, pure names, with nothing underneath them of what they signify of the meaning of divinity, nothing at all. That is, they have no share of it except the application of those names to them.

Al-Shihab said: The intended meaning is that they have no share at all, and there is no justification for naming them thus. Had divinity been realized merely by naming, they would be gods. So this is the negation of a thing by affirming it, or it is a pure claim with no substance beneath it.

﴿that you have named﴾, that is, you made them names while they are empty of the things named. ﴿you and your fathers﴾, that is, according to your whims and the imitation of the follower of the one followed. ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾, that is, no proof on which they rest. ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾, that is, they only imagine that what they are upon is true. ﴿and what their souls desire﴾, that is, what their souls crave.

Ibn Jarir said: Because they did not take this from a revelation that came to them from God, nor from a messenger of God who informed them of it. Rather, it is a fabrication from their own selves, or they took it from their fathers, who were in disbelief in God in the same manner as they are. ﴿Though guidance has already come to them from their Lord﴾, that is, the clear proof and the explanation through revelation that worshipping them is not fitting, and that worship is appropriate only to Him, the Exalted, alone.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of ﴿they follow﴾, or a parenthetical interjection (i'tiradh). Whichever it is, it affirms the invalidity of following conjecture and the desires of the soul, and increases the censure of their condition, for following these two is ugly from anyone at all, and from one whom God has guided by sending the Messenger (ﷺ) and sending down the Books, it is uglier still.

**Note:**

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): It has been cited as evidence, by His saying ﴿They are but names﴾ and so on, that languages are tawqifiyyah (divinely ordained, i.e., originating from revelation rather than human convention). The reasoning is that He censured them for naming some things with what they named them, and if naming other things were not from God by tawqif, this censure would not be valid, since all of it would be convention on their part.

It has also been cited, by His saying ﴿they follow nothing but conjecture﴾ and so on, as evidence for the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation) in matters of belief. The Zahiriyyah (the literalist school) used it to invalidate taqlid absolutely, or to invalidate qiyas (analogical reasoning).

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Umar who said: Beware of this opinion (ra'y) in religion, for opinion from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was correct only because God was showing it to him, whereas from us it is merely an effort and conjecture. ﴿Surely conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28]. End.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 53, verse 24:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[24] ﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾

﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾ That is: it is not the case that he obtains whatever he desires of matters, among which is his vain hope for the intercession of rivals (andad), his obstinate insistence on defending certainty with conjecture (zann), and his leaving himself and his desires without a law (shar') to restrain him or a guardian (muhaymin) to hold him back. For that is among the impossibilities in the view of sound reason, like His saying: ﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾ [al-Nisa': 123].

The commentary on His saying, exalted is He:

[25] ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾

﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ That is: the final outcome of the matter in both of them belongs to Him, exalted is He, not to man, according to what his commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara bi-l-su') embellishes for him. As He said: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 71]. For this reason He sent the messengers to him and sent down the books, as a cutting off of excuses, and He alerted him, through reason, to the paths of happiness which are not hidden from one who sees clearly.

The discussion of the words of His exalted saying:

[26] ﴿How many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves.﴾

This is a rebuke from Allah, exalted is He, directed at the worshippers of idols, by despairing them of what they had set their hopes upon regarding the intercession of their idols, since His noble angels do not utter a word of intercession except after His permission and approval. How then could these tyrannical idols presume to usurp this station, when they have such abasement and humiliation that keeps them a thousand stations away from it?

Then he pointed to another form of arrogance of the polytheists, by the words of His glorified saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 53, verse 27:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[27] ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females.﴾ That is, with the naming of females. This is because they used to say, "They are the daughters of Allah." Thus *al-unthā* (الأنثى, "the female") is taken in the sense of *al-ināth* (الإناث, "females"), since it is a collective noun (*ism jins*) that applies to both the many and the few. It has also been said that it means "the female group." It has also been said that it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, as a comparison, so there is no need to make it plural. It has also been said that it is singular for the sake of the verse-ending (*fāṣila*, the rhyming end of the verse). And it has been said that *al-malā'ika* (الملائكة, "the angels") carries the sense of encompassing each individual, meaning: they name each one of them a daughter, and this is the naming of a female, in the pattern of "the amir clothed us a robe" (*kasānā al-amīru ḥullatan*), meaning he clothed each one of us a robe. The singular form is used because there is no ambiguity.

Abu al-Su'ud said: In linking it to not believing in the Hereafter there is an indication that this (naming) is so abominable and monstrous, and entails punishment in the Hereafter, that none would dare to do it except one who does not believe in it at all.

(p-٥٥٧٩)

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[28–29] ﴿Yet they have no knowledge of it. They follow only conjecture, and indeed conjecture avails nothing against the truth at all.﴾ ﴿So turn away from those who turn away from Our remembrance and desire nothing but the life of this world.﴾ [An-Najm: 29]

﴿Yet they have no knowledge of it. They follow only conjecture, and indeed conjecture avails nothing against the truth at all.﴾ That is: it does not provide the benefit of knowledge, nor does it take its place. This is because the reality of a thing and what it is in itself is only grasped with a grasp that is reliable when it is based on certainty, not on conjecture and supposition.

﴿So turn away from those who turn away from Our remembrance and desire nothing but the life of this world.﴾ [An-Najm: 29] That is: from these disbelievers, who consider the goal of their happiness to be enjoying its pleasures, because their vision is limited to what is perceptible to the senses. What is meant by "turning away" (al-i'rad) is abandoning them in a gracious manner and leaving off harming them. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement: "That is: turn away from calling those whom you see turning away from the remembrance of Allah... etc.," it is not correct, because proclaiming the truth admits no leniency, especially since the call is directed to those who turn away, and it requires that they be argued with using every possible effort, according to His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And strive against them with it, a great striving﴾ [Al-Furqan: 52]. Rather, the meaning of the verse is: pardon them and leave aside their harm, in return for what they inflict on you through their ignorance, as He has clarified in several places of the revelation, and the Qur'an explains one part of it by another.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[30] ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge. Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided.﴾

﴿That is the extent of their knowledge﴾ means: the affair of this world is the limit of their knowledge; they have no knowledge beyond it. And whoever has this as the furthest of his understanding, there is nothing for his caller [to do] except to pardon him and to be patient with his ignorance.

"Mablagh" (extent, limit) is, by way of metaphor, a noun of place, as if it were a location in which their knowledge came to a halt, by way of claim, as al-Shihab (al-Alusi) verified. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) affirming the content of what precedes it, namely the restriction of their aim to the life of this world. Then He gave the reason for turning away from them with His saying, glorified is He:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided.﴾ That is: and He must deal with them according to what His knowledge requires concerning them, recompensing each according to what his deeds necessitate. The mention of knowledge concerning those who stray is given precedence because they are the intended addressees of the discourse and the context concerns them. And His saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 53, verse 31:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[31] ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil with what they did and recompense those who did good with the best (reward).﴾

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is a reminder of the vastness of His dominion and the greatness of His power, and that whatever is in them is within His grasp, so the recompense of these wicked ones cannot overwhelm Him. As He said: ﴿that He may recompense those who did evil with what they did and recompense those who did good with the best﴾, i.e., with the best reward, which is Paradise. Then He explained the attributes of these good-doers by His saying, glorified is He:

القَوْلُ في تَأْوِيلِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى:

[٣٢] ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses. Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness. He knows you best, since He brought you forth from the earth and when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers. So do not claim your own purity; He knows best who fears Him.﴾

﴿Those who avoid the major sins﴾ meaning those whose threat of punishment is great among the prohibited acts, and ﴿immoralities﴾ meaning what is grossly evil among them. The conjunction is either between two synonyms, or the specific is joined to the general. ﴿Except for minor lapses﴾ meaning the small sins. Abu Hurayra illustrated them with a kiss, a squeeze, and a glance, as narrated by Ibn Jarir (p-٥٥٨١). The original meaning of the word is that whose extent is small, and from it comes "lamma" of hair, because it is less than the full "wafra." It was said that it means drawing near to something without committing it. The exception (al-istithna', i.e., the grammatical exception) is disjunctive according to what has been mentioned. It was said that "lamam" is what falls below the major sins and immoralities, for it is forgiven. It was said that the exception is connected, and that the intended meaning is sins in general. It was said that there is no exception in it at all, and that "illa" is an adjective meaning "ghayr" (other than). Its detailed discussion is in al-'Inaya.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas and others that the meaning of "lamam" is what has already passed for them of immoralities and major sins in the Jahiliyya, before Islam, and that He forgave them when they embraced Islam.

Also from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: it is the man who commits an immorality and then repents and does not return to it. He said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"O Allah, if You forgive, You forgive abundantly, and which of Your servants does not commit lapses?"

Al-Hasan said: "lamam" is that a person commits the act and then desists.

All of this is encompassed by the noble wording, and the strongest of these meanings is the first. Therefore the verse was used as evidence that minor sins are expiated by avoiding the major sins, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you avoid the major of what you are forbidden, We will expiate from you your bad deeds﴾ [al-Nisa: 31].

﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾. Ibn Jarir said: that is, vast in His pardon for the sinners whose sins have not reached the immoralities and major sins. ﴿He knows you best, since He brought you forth from the earth﴾. Ibn Jarir said: that is, He brought you into being from it, through the creation of your father Adam from it. ﴿And when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers﴾, that is, wherever He shapes you in the wombs. ﴿So do not claim your own purity﴾, that is, do not testify for yourselves that you are pure and free of sins and acts of disobedience; the intended meaning is praise, whether out of self-admiration or showing off. ﴿He knows best who fears Him﴾, that is, who fears Him, obeys Him, avoids His disobedience, and sets things right. This is like His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged even a thread-width﴾ [al-Nisa: 49].

In the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn, i.e., the collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim), from Abu Bakra, he said: "A man praised another man in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Woe to you! You have cut off the neck of your companion,' repeating it several times. 'If one of you must praise his companion, let him say: I think so-and-so is such, and Allah is his reckoner, and I do not claim purity for anyone before Allah; I think him to be such-and-such, if he knows that.'"

The discussion of the words of Allah, the Exalted:

[38] ﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾

﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾: that is, no soul is held to account for the sin of another; rather, every sinner, its sin is upon itself.

Al-Qashani said: Because punishment follows from dark states that become firmly rooted in the soul through the repetition of evil deeds and evil sayings, which are sins. Likewise, reward follows only from their opposites, the states of virtue, as Allah the Exalted said:

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[39] ﴿And that there is not for man except what he strives for.﴾

﴿And that there is not for man except what he strives for﴾ means: except his striving and his earning.

Remarks:

First: Ibn Jarir said: By His words ﴿That no bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Najm: 38], He meant the one who guaranteed to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira that he would bear his punishment on the Day of Resurrection. He says: Has not the speaker of this statement, and the guarantor of this guarantee, been informed of what is written in the scriptures of Musa and Ibrahim: that no sinner shall bear the sin of another, ﴿and that there is not for man except what he strives for﴾, meaning: and that no doer is recompensed except for his deed, whether good or evil. End of quotation.

The apparent context indicates that the verses were revealed in refutation of what they conjectured, what they wished for, and what they judged about the unseen out of obstinacy and ignorance. Nevertheless, their comprehensive meaning is clear.

Second: al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): It has been cited as evidence that proxy (niyabah) does not apply in acts of worship, for the living or the dead. Al-Shafi'i used it as evidence that the reward of recitation does not reach the dead. End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: From this noble verse, al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and those who followed him derived that the gift of the reward of recitation does not reach the dead, because it is not of their striving nor of their earning. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not recommend it to his community, nor urge them to it, nor guide them to it by explicit text or allusion, and this was not reported from any of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Had it been good, they would have preceded us to it. The domain of acts of devotion is confined to the texts and is not handled by kinds of analogies and opinions. As for supplication and charity, these are agreed upon as reaching the dead, and the Lawgiver has stated them explicitly.

As for the hadith narrated by Muslim in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When a person dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: a righteous child who prays for him, or ongoing charity after him, or knowledge from which benefit is derived." These three are in reality part of his striving, his effort and his work, as came in the hadith: "Indeed, the best food a man eats is from his earnings, and indeed his child is from his earnings." Ongoing charity, such as an endowment (waqf) and the like, is among the fruits of his work and his endowment, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Indeed, We bring the dead to life and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12]. And the knowledge he spread among people, so that people followed him after him, is also part of his striving and work.

It is established in the two Sahihs: "Whoever calls to guidance will have a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without that diminishing their rewards in the least." End of quotation.

Third: al-Razi said: The purpose of the verse is to explain the reward of righteous deeds, or to explain every deed. We say: the well-known view is that it applies to every deed, so good is rewarded for and evil is requited by it. The apparent meaning is that it explains the good deeds, as indicated by the preposition "lam" (for/to) in His words ﴿li-l-insani﴾ (for man), for "lam" indicates the return of benefits, while "ʿala" (upon) indicates the return of harms. You say: this is for him, and this is against him; and it testifies for him, and it testifies against him, regarding benefits and harms. The first speaker may respond that when both matters are combined, the more excellent prevails, as with the sound plural masculine form which is used when females are combined with males. Also indicating this is His words ﴿Then he will be recompensed with the fullest recompense﴾ [al-Najm: 41], and "the fullest" (al-awfa) applies only in return for a good deed; as for an evil deed, the requital is its equivalent or less, or pardon altogether. End of quotation.

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[57–58] ﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near.﴾ ﴿None besides Allah can disclose it.﴾ [al-Najm: 58]

﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near﴾, i.e., the Resurrection, which is described as near, has come close. The definite article in al-Azifah (the Imminent) is for prior reference (li-l-ʿahd). It has also been said that al-Azifah is here a proper designation (ʿalam bi-l-ghalabah) for the Hour, so that the near is not described as near (li-allā yalzama wasf al-qarīb bi-l-qarīb).

(p-5589) Al-Shihab said: "This is open to question, because describing the near by nearness conveys emphasis on its proximity, just as the form of the reflexive verb (al-iftiʿal) indicates in ﴿has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1]."

﴿None besides Allah can disclose it﴾ [al-Najm: 58], i.e., none other than Allah makes clear its time for its coming, as in His words: ﴿None reveals it at its time except Him﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 187]. ﴿Disclosing﴾ [kashifah, al-Najm: 58] is an adjective of an omitted noun, i.e., "a soul disclosing," or "a state disclosing," or the ta' is for emphasis (li-l-mubalaghah). Or it is a verbal noun (masdar) formed with the feminine ending, and "besides Allah" means "other than Allah," or "except Allah." It has also been said that the disclosing (al-kashf) means removal (al-izalah), i.e., no soul will be able to remove it when it befalls, except Him, exalted is He, from the expression "disclosing the distress" (kashf al-ghammaʾ).

**The explanation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse?﴾ ﴿And you laugh and do not weep?﴾ [53:59–60] ﴿while you are proud and heedless?﴾ [53:61] ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him].﴾ [53:62]

﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse﴾ means the Qur'an, which relates what came before and warns with what it has announced. ﴿You wonder﴾ means a wondering of denial, even though what it contains compels submission and affirmation, and indeed, because of its truth, abundant tears flow. As He said, ﴿And you laugh﴾ [53:60], that is, in mockery. ﴿And do not weep﴾ [53:60], that is, at what it contains of threat for the disobedient, and at what you have neglected before hearing its reminder, as those who are certain of it do. He described them in the verse: ﴿They fall down upon their faces, weeping, and it increases them in humility﴾ [17:109]. ﴿While you are proud﴾ [53:61], that is, heedless of what it contains of lessons, turning away from its signs out of arrogance.

Mujahid said: They used to pass by the Prophet ﷺ angry and mubarthimin, meaning lofty (haughty).

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is singing: when they heard the Qur'an they would sing and play. This is the dialect of the people of Yemen, who say "*usmud lana*" (اسْمُدْ لَنا), meaning "sing for us." The outcome is one, although the expression differs. There is no doubt that all of this was issuing from the polytheists.

In *al-Iklil* it is said: In it is the recommendation of weeping during recitation, and the blame of laughing, singing, amusement, play, and heedlessness, just as the word ﴿samidun﴾ [53:61] was explained with these four. Al-Suddi explained it as arrogance.

﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾ [53:62], that is, worship Him alone, to the exclusion of whatever else of the idols, for worship should belong to none but Him, so do not set up any partner with Him in His worship.

On the authority of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The first surah in which a prostration was revealed was *al-Najm* [53:1]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prostrated, and whoever was behind him prostrated..." and the hadith [continues]. It has preceded at the beginning of the surah.

Imam Ahmad related from al-Muttalib ibn Wada'a, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited *Surat al-Najm* in Makkah, and prostrated, and whoever was with him prostrated. I raised my head and refused to prostrate—al-Muttalib had not embraced Islam on that day—and after that, he would not hear anyone recite it without prostrating with him." It was also related by al-Nasa'i.

Imam Ahmad related from al-Muttalib ibn Wada'a, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited *Surat al-Najm* in Makkah, and prostrated, and whoever was with him prostrated. I raised my head and refused to prostrate—al-Muttalib had not embraced Islam on that day—and after that, he would not hear anyone recite it without prostrating with him." It was also related by al-Nasa'i.
